title: Miguel Pro (23 November)
hook: a Mexican Jesuit shot with his arms stretched out, saying long live Christ the King

segments.voice: Yesterday, Columban, the Irish monk who left home on purpose. Your line was pilgrim for christ. Did you take a different road somewhere? Day one thousand forty-eight.

A yard in Mexico City. A wall. A line of men with rifles. A priest in a plain suit is walked out to stand in front of them. According to the accounts handed down, he asks for one thing: a moment to pray. He kneels. He prays. Then he gets up, and instead of folding his hands or bracing himself, he stretches his arms out wide, the shape of a cross, and says a few words in Spanish. Those words are today's line. The man is Miguel Pro.
screen: `A YARD, A WALL, A LINE OF RIFLES.` → `HE KNEELS TO PRAY.` → `ARMS STRETCHED WIDE.`

segments.voice: Miguel Pro was a Jesuit priest at a time when the Mexican government had turned hard against the Church. Public worship stopped. Priests who stayed did their work in secret. Pro stayed. The stories told about him are full of disguises: a mechanic in overalls, a beggar, a well-dressed young man strolling past the police. He said Mass in private houses, heard confessions, and carried communion to people who couldn't get to a church. The stories are also full of jokes; he seems to have been funny, even in hiding. Then came a failed attack on a former president, and Pro and his brothers were arrested. The accounts say he had no part in it, and that he was shot without a trial. Now look at his last moment, because it was a prayer made with the body. He knelt first. Then he stood with his arms out. The posture is the shape of the cross. And the accounts say he forgave the men in front of him, which echoes what Jesus says from the cross in Luke's gospel. In the Douay-Rheims: "Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do." The accounts give his last words as the cry of persecuted Catholics in Mexico in those years: viva Cristo Rey. Long live Christ the King. It isn't a curse on anyone. It's a statement about who rules. The soldiers held the rifles; he named a different king. The Church declared him blessed, and in some places his day is kept on 23 November, close to the feast of Christ the King.
screen: `A PRIEST IN HIDING, IN DISGUISE.` · `ARRESTED, SHOT WITHOUT A TRIAL.` · `ARMS OUT: A PRAYER MADE WITH THE BODY.` · `HE NAMED A DIFFERENT KING.` · then, large: `VIVA CRISTO REY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray with your arms. Stand or sit up straight. Slowly stretch your arms out to the sides, palms open, as wide as feels easy. Hold them there while you take a few slow breaths, and notice how open, and how unprotected, the body feels. When your arms tire, lower them and rest your hands on your knees, palms up. If you pray, you can say the three words, viva Cristo Rey, quietly, once. If you don't, just stay with the open hands. The bell holds the time.
Miguel Pro. The Jesuit who served in disguise while churches were closed, and who died with his arms out, naming Christ as King.
Your line: viva cristo rey. Today, when something tries to run your whole mood, open your hands for a second, the way he did, and let it go by. Day one thousand forty-eight.

howItsDone: Blessed Miguel Agustín Pro is remembered on 23 November in some local calendars, including in Mexico and the United States, and Catholics there often pray for those who suffer for their faith.

notes: Audit (fresh pass): Luke 23:34 Douay-Rheims checked; arrest with his brothers, execution without trial, arms outstretched and last words attributed to the accounts. No change.
The index hook names the year (1927); the year is left out of the script and the hook line under the claims rule. Keeper may restore it if the cited account is added.

Disguises, private Masses, his humor, arrest with his brothers after the attack on Obregón (left unnamed), execution without trial, kneeling, outstretched arms, forgiving the firing squad and 'Viva Cristo Rey': all from devotional and Jesuit accounts; confirm each detail.
'Public worship stopped': the suspension of public worship by the bishops in response to the Calles laws; confirm the simplified phrasing.
'The cry of persecuted Catholics in Mexico in those years': confirm; avoided tying it to armed Cristero fighting.
Beatification stated without a date. Confirm his memorial is kept on 23 November in the US proper calendar and in Mexico.

Editor pass: 'Christians would have read that posture at once' (a claim about what people thought) replaced with a plain description; his last words now attributed to the accounts rather than stated as fact.
